title: Family
intro: Meeting and visiting your partner's family: forms of address, gifts, dinner, small talk and festivals.

scenes.title: Meeting your partner's parents: what to call them and what to say
scenes.description: How to address your partner's parents before marriage (叔叔/阿姨, or 伯父/伯母) and after the wedding (改口 to 爸/妈, usually at the wedding tea ceremony, with the 改口费 gift), short polite lines for a first visit, and what the hosts will say to you. Evidence: CC-CEDICT, the 现代汉语词典 transcription, official HSK/YCT papers and syllabi, Tatoeba sentences, Xinhua data, relationship.js, and (for current etiquette) a few web articles read through search-result summaries.

phrases.english: Uncle — what you call your partner's father (or any man of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: Before marriage a friend's or partner's parents are 叔叔 and 阿姨: in the official HSK 3 sample paper a man about to marry tells a friend '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来' (bring your parents — lit. uncle and auntie — along too). CC-CEDICT: 'form of address used by children for a male one generation older'; Xinhua: '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子' (general term for men of one's father's generation who are younger [than one's father]); for a man clearly older than your own father the matching title is 伯父/伯伯. Pair it with 您: HSK 3 sample '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？'. Children will in turn call you 叔叔 if you are a man of their parents' generation. Whether your partner's family expects 叔叔 or 伯父 is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Auntie — what you call your partner's mother (or any woman of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: The counterpart of 叔叔 (HSK 3 sample: '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来'). Xinhua: '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女：王～' (address for a woman of one's mother's generation and similar age, e.g. 王阿姨); CC-CEDICT: 'woman of similar age to one's parents (term of address used by child)'. HSK 5 sample: '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？' (a young man to a retired woman, with 您). 阿姨 is also how nannies and childcare workers are addressed (Xinhua sense ③; CC-CEDICT 'childcare worker; nursemaid'). Alternative pair: 伯父/伯母.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Xinhua marks only the kinship sense 'mother's sister' as dialectal (〈方〉); the title sense (王阿姨) has no regional label.

phrases.english: Hello, Auntie! (polite greeting with title)
phrases.usage: Title first, then the polite hello 您好 (CC-CEDICT: 'hello (polite)'; 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'). Adapted by one slot change from official HSK samples that put a title before 您好: '刘先生您好' (HSK 6) and '王教授您好，路上辛苦了。' (HSK 5). Swap the title for the person you greet (slot).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: the title of the person you greet

phrases.english: Sorry to bother you. / Sorry for the trouble.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'sorry to interrupt you, but ... / sorry to have bothered you / sorry, I have to go'. In the HSK 4 sample a visitor who did not find the person ends with '好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。'. So it fits when you interrupt someone and when you take your leave after imposing on them. CC-CEDICT also lists a slang sense (coined c. 2017, mostly online): said facetiously to end a conversation with someone insufferable — your tone makes the difference.

phrases.english: Thank you for your warm hospitality.
phrases.usage: A guest's thanks to the hosts. In the HSK 5 sample it is the guest's reply to the hosts' welcome at a dinner they give ('您好，王经理，欢迎来参加我们的宴会。' — '谢谢你们的热情招待。'); another HSK 5 sample has '谢谢你们的招待，…' at a banquet. 你们 = both of you / your family. CC-CEDICT 招待: 'to offer hospitality; to entertain (guests)'. Both samples are business dinners; the wording itself is not business-specific.

phrases.english: Your grandpa looks very young.
phrases.usage: Compliment from the YCT 4 sample ('你爷爷看上去很年轻。' — reply: '他身体不错，每天都坚持散步两个小时。'), said to your partner about a relative; swap the relative (slot). 看起来 works the same way (Tatoeba: '她看起来很年轻。'). To the person directly: 阿姨，您看起来真年轻！ (separate item). 你妈 is normal inside a sentence (Tatoeba: '你和你妈用上海话聊天的时候…'), but as a bare exclamation it is a curse (CC-CEDICT), so 你妈妈 sounds gentler when you speak of your partner's mother. CC-CEDICT 看上去: 'it would appear; it seems (that)'.
phrases.speaker: me

Swap the relative (slot) to praise another family member; say 你妈妈 in full — CC-CEDICT lists 你妈 on its own as a vulgar interjection. CC-CEDICT 看上去: 'it would appear; it seems (that)'.".

phrases.english: Don't stand on ceremony. / No need to be so polite. / Don't mention it.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'don't mention it / no formalities, please'. Hosts say it when you are being very polite; a guest can use it to wave away help or an offer: HSK 5 sample '不用，别客气，我的包不重，我自己来。' (refusing help with a bag); YCT 4 sample '谢谢王老师，您别客气，我刚喝了茶，不渴。' (declining a drink, to an elder, with 您). 不用客气 means the same (CC-CEDICT: 'you're welcome / don't mention it / no need to stand on ceremony').
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Uncle (respectful) — title for a man of your father's generation who is older than your own father
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'father's elder brother; term of respect for older man'. As a title it strictly suits a man older than your own father (Xinhua defines 叔叔 as the term for the younger ones). HSK 2025 lists 伯父/伯伯/伯母 at level 7-9 and 叔叔/阿姨 at level 3. Whether your partner's family prefers 伯父/伯母 or 叔叔/阿姨 at a first visit is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: As a title for a partner's father, 伯父 is understood everywhere. Don't carry over the northern kinship word 大爷 (= your own father's older brother in the north; see the paternal chart): said to an unrelated man, 大爷 is a title for an old man (现代汉语词典 大爷 ❷ '尊称年长的男子').

phrases.english: Mum — how you address your partner's mother once you are married
phrases.usage: After the wedding you 改口 (change how you address them): CC-CEDICT 改口 '…as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈'; 改口费 is given to the new daughter-in-law or son-in-law, so the switch concerns both. 妈 is the everyday short form; with 您 it stays respectful, as in the HSK 4 sample '妈，您的手机响了。'. Before the 改口, use 阿姨 (or 伯母). The switch usually happens at the wedding, during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶) when the parents hand over the 改口费; some families invite you to say 妈 earlier (for example once you are engaged or have registered the marriage) — wait for them to offer, and follow your partner's lead.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Hello, Uncle and Auntie! (greeting your partner's parents when you arrive)
phrases.usage: The usual greeting at the door: the title + 好, both parents at once — a ChinesePod lesson set at a girlfriend's parents' home opens with '叔叔阿姨好', and a maigoo.com article advises 叔叔阿姨 until the couple is engaged. Greeting each one separately (叔叔好！阿姨好！) works too — the same pattern as 大家好！ ('hello, everyone'). If the parents are older than your own parents, 伯父伯母好！ is the respectful variant. Then give your name (see 我叫…).
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.pinyin_as_source: CC-CEDICT 添麻烦: tian1 ma2 fan5; HSK 2025: 添 tiān (level 6), 麻烦 máfan (level 4)
phrases.english: Sorry to put you to so much trouble. / Thank you for going to all this trouble.
phrases.usage: A guest's apology-cum-thanks when the hosts have gone out of their way — cooked a big meal, fetched you from the station, put you up for the night. Tatoeba: '给你添麻烦了，真的非常抱歉。' (I'm very sorry to have troubled you); 现代汉语词典 麻烦: '给你添了不少～' and the shorter '～您啦！' (= 麻烦您了！, Tatoeba 'Sorry to bother you!'). Use 您 for one parent; for both, 给你们添麻烦了 or 给叔叔阿姨添麻烦了 (slot).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: the person or people you have put to trouble

rules.rule: Speak to your partner's parents (and other elders) with 您, the courteous 'you', and put their title first: 叔叔，您…; 阿姨，您好. After marriage 您 stays respectful (妈，您…), but follow your partner's lead: many families, especially in the south, say 你 to their own parents.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'. The official HSK samples show younger speakers pairing titles with 您: '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？', '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？', '妈，您的手机响了。', '爸，您为什么要问我这么简单的问题？'. (Some samples show children using 你 with their own parents, e.g. the answer option '爸爸，你累了吧'; for an in-law, 您 is the courteous form.)
rules.regional_note: 您 is far more frequent in northern speech (Beijing above all); in the south many people say 你 even to elders in everyday talk, so 您 can sound a little formal there — but it is never wrong at a first meeting (anecdotal evidence: learner-forum reports).

rules.rule: Before marriage — and especially before you are engaged — call your partner's parents by kinship titles, as you would a friend's parents: 叔叔 (father) and 阿姨 (mother), greeting them with 叔叔阿姨好; or 伯父/伯母 if they are older than your own parents. Surname + title (王阿姨, 张叔叔) is the standard pattern for other older acquaintances, such as neighbours and family friends.
rules.why: HSK 3 sample: a man invites a friend's parents to his wedding as '叔叔、阿姨'. Xinhua: 阿姨 = '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女'; 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. CC-CEDICT: 伯父 'term of respect for older man', 伯母 'polite form of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother'. HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'.

rules.rule: For men of your father's generation, 叔叔 fits those younger than your own father and 伯伯/伯父 those older. Within the family their wives are 婶婶 and 伯母; outside the family the usual title for a woman of your parents' generation is 阿姨 (伯母 goes with 伯父).
rules.why: Xinhua: 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. rules.rule: Do not call your partner's parents (or other elders) by their names; use their title.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 直呼其名: 'to address sb directly by name; to address sb by name without using an honorific title (indicating familiarity or overfamiliarity)'. The HSK 2025 syllabus teaches titles — 姓氏+职业（张老师）、姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）— as the appropriate forms of address.

rules.rule: 改口: you switch to 爸/妈 (爸爸/妈妈) for your partner's parents at the wedding, usually during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶), and they give you 改口费. Before that use 叔叔/阿姨 (or 伯父/伯母), and don't start saying 爸/妈 on your own initiative: some parents invite it earlier (after the engagement or the marriage registration), and then you follow their lead.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 改口: '…to change the way one addresses sb (as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈)'; 改口费: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. 现代汉语词典/Xinhua 改口 ②: '改变称呼'. Web articles (search summaries): '敬茶又叫"改口茶"…当双方父母喝下新人们敬的茶后，还会给新人们改口费'; '若是两人还没有开始谈婚论嫁…就喊叔叔阿姨是最好的' (maigoo); parents who accept you may say you can call them 爸/媽 (Marie Claire Taiwan); following one's spouse in calling the in-laws 爸爸/媽媽 is still widespread (ETtoday, 2026).
rules.regional_note: Who gives 改口费, and how much, varies by region and family — in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner.

rules.rule: 公公/婆婆 (husband's parents) and 岳父/岳母 (wife's parents) name the relationship; once married you address them as 爸/妈. Before the wedding they are not yet your 公婆 or 岳父母.

The dictionary flags a parallel case explicitly: 小姨子 '(term not used to directly address her)'.

rules.rule: Kinship words double as polite titles for people who are not relatives: 叔叔/阿姨 for your parents' generation, surname + 爷爷 (张爷爷) for the grandparents' generation, 大哥/大姐 for people somewhat older than you, 大叔/大姨 for people about your parents' age.
rules.why: HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'. Xinhua: 爷爷 sense 3 '对男性尊长的称呼'. CC-CEDICT: 大哥 'polite address for a man of about the same age as oneself', 大姐 'polite term of address for a girl or woman slightly older than the speaker', 大叔 'term used to address a man about the age of one's father', 大姨 'respectful term of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother', 大娘 'aunt (polite address)'.
rules.regional_note: relationship.js readme: 大爷 can mean grandfather's elder brother or, in the north, father's elder brother. CC-CEDICT 大爷 dàye is also a 'term of respect for older man' — but dàyé (full second tone) means 'arrogant idler'.

scenes.title: First visit: arriving and giving gifts
scenes.description: Arriving at your partner's parents' home for the first time: greeting them, handing over gifts modestly, the polite refusal exchange, and being offered tea. NOTE: gift taboos (clocks, pears, umbrellas, etc.) and what to bring could not be verified in this session (see open_questions).

phrases.pinyin_as_source: shū•shu, āyí (XDHYCD headwords; the syllabus gives no pinyin)
phrases.english: Hello, Uncle! Hello, Auntie! (greeting your partner's father and mother)
phrases.usage: Greeting pattern "(称谓)+好！" (address term + 好) from the official function list, section 打招呼 (greeting). 叔叔 and 阿姨 are the dictionary-standard ways to address a man / a woman of your parents' generation who is not your relative; an HSK 3 sample dialogue uses 叔叔、阿姨 for (most likely) a friend's parents. Say it when you arrive, before handing over gifts. Slot: the address term; check with your partner which term the family expects (see the address-term rule below).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: address term (称谓) for the person you greet

phrases.regional_note: XDHYCD: strictly 叔叔 is for men younger than your own father and 伯伯/伯父 for men older than him; which term this family expects is a family/regional habit not researched here: ask your partner.

phrases.english: This is for you.
phrases.usage: Said while handing over a present. Built from the official pattern "(某礼物)+是送给你的" (gift + 是送给你的) in section 14. 馈赠 (gift-giving): the gift slot is 这 "this", and 您 (respectful "you") replaces 你 because you are speaking to your partner's parents (slot change). Same structure in an HSK 2 sample ("生日快乐！这是我送给你的。") and on Tatoeba ("这份礼物是送给你的。").

phrases.english: Just a small token (of my regard).
phrases.usage: A fixed modest formula listed in the official function list under 14. 馈赠 (gift-giving); say it as you hand over the gift, often after 这是送给您的. XDHYCD defines 心意 as "对人的情意" (kind feelings towards someone). The same list gives a much more formal "……，不成敬意，请笑纳" (it is not much, please accept it), and XDHYCD calls 笑纳 a 客套话 for asking someone to accept a gift. The wording "一点小心意" that is often quoted was NOT found in any source in this session; the attested forms are 一点儿心意 and 一点儿小意思.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: The 儿 is optional (XDHYCD writes 一点（儿））; 一点心意 without erhua is also correct. Follow the family's own habit.

phrases.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ cóng Hélán dàilái de tèchǎn, nín chángchang ba.
phrases.literal: this is I from Netherlands bring-come DE specialty, you (polite) taste-taste BA
phrases.english: This is a specialty I brought from the Netherlands, please try it.
phrases.usage: ADAPTED, not verbatim: the HSK 5 sample sentence is "这是我从海南带回来的特产，你尝尝吧。" (said by someone back from a trip to Hainan). Changes: place slot 海南 -> 荷兰; 你 -> 您; and 带回来 "brought back" -> 带来 "brought" (as in Tatoeba "从中国带来的龙井茶"), because XDHYCD defines 回来 as coming back to where one started — keep 带回来 only if you are returning home. XDHYCD: 特产 = a product special to a place or country, so it fits Dutch food specialties (尝尝 = have a taste; use it for food or drink only). Pinyin: CC-CEDICT has no entry 尝尝; the second syllable of a reduplicated one-syllable verb is neutral, as in CC-CEDICT 看看 kànkan.

phrases.hanzi: 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ de xīnyì wǒ lǐng le, dàn lǐwù wúlùnrúhé bù néng shōu.
phrases.literal: your heart-intention I receive-LE, but gift in-any-case cannot accept
phrases.english: I appreciate the thought, but I really can't accept the gift.
phrases.usage: A fixed formula for declining a gift, listed under 47. 拒绝 (declining) in the official list (next to "这种礼物绝对不能收"). Dictionary variants: "我领这个情，但东西不能收。" (XDHYCD 领情) and "您的美意，我心领了。" (XDHYCD 心领: 客套话 used to decline a gift or a meal). You will hear it rather than say it. The words alone do not tell you whether the refusal is ritual or real; ask your partner how hard to insist.

rules.rule: When you hand over a gift, your hosts may first protest politely (客气) before accepting it. Fixed formulas for declining gifts exist (你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 / 我领这个情，但东西不能收 / 您的美意，我心领了), and a dictionary example describes the whole sequence: 他客气了一番，把礼物收下了 "he made polite protests, then accepted the gift". Present the gift modestly (一点儿心意 / 一点儿小意思) and ask them to accept it (请收下这份小礼物吧).
rules.why: Modesty on both sides is built into the standard gift vocabulary: the official function list has separate entries for giving (馈赠), accepting (接受) and declining (拒绝) gifts, and XDHYCD labels 心领 and 笑纳 as 客套话 (polite formulas). How many times to insist, and when a refusal is real, is not stated in these sources.

rules.rule: Address your partner's parents with a title. The dictionary-standard titles for unrelated people of your parents' generation are 叔叔 (a man; strictly one younger than your own father) or 伯伯/伯父 (a man older than your father), and 阿姨 (a woman). Use 您 when you speak to them.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 叔叔❷, 伯父❷ and 阿姨❷ as forms of address for non-relatives of the parents' generation; 您 is "你 (含敬意)", the respectful you.
rules.regional_note: XDHYCD marks the "mother's sister" sense of 阿姨 as dialectal (方), and marks 外婆/外公 (maternal grandparents) as dialectal while 姥姥/姥爷 are unmarked standard forms. Which titles this south/central-China family uses is not documented here: ask your partner (the family address-term topic covers this in detail).

phrases.english: Please don't see me out.
phrases.usage: Guest to host who walks you to the door or beyond (official list: "[客人]：别送了/您留步"). XDHYCD 留步 is the more formal 客套话 for the same thing ("used by a guest asking the host not to see them out"): 您留步. An HSK 5 dialogue shows the host insisting anyway: guest "不用送了，赶紧回去吧，家里还有别的客人呢。" — host "没关系，已经出来了，就送到公交站吧。"

rules.rule: Chopstick manners: while talking, do not wave your chopsticks around; do not tap bowls, plates or the table with them; never point at people with them; when you put them down during the meal, lay them on the table or on the edge of your plate and never stick them (upright) into the rice bowl; avoid making noise with them.
rules.why: Stated in an official HSK 5 reading passage: "筷子……在使用上也有很多讲究。用餐过程中，如果说话，不要将筷子随便晃动，也不要用筷子敲打碗、盘子以及桌面，更不能用筷子指点他人，暂时离开时，要把筷子轻轻放在桌子上或餐盘边，不能插在饭碗里，而且尽量不要发出响声。" (the keyed answer is "说话时敲筷子不礼貌"). Use of serving chopsticks (公筷, CC-CEDICT "serving chopsticks") was not verified as current practice (open question).

rules.rule: When you toast someone (敬酒), keep your glass low (敬酒时杯子放低).
rules.why: An official BCT (Business Chinese Test) sample listening question offers "A 可随意就座 B 用筷子敲杯子 C 倒茶时倒满杯子 D 敬酒时杯子放低", and the answer key gives D ("when toasting, keep your glass low"). The audio text of the question is not in the printed paper, so the exact wording is unknown; the three other options are probably things the passage advises against (sitting anywhere, tapping cups with chopsticks, filling tea to the brim), but that is an inference. The printed text also does not say "lower than the other person's glass"; check the detail with your partner.

rules.rule: 干杯 literally means "drain the cup": it is used to urge others to drink or to celebrate, so a 干杯 aimed at you can mean that you are expected to empty your glass.
rules.why: XDHYCD: "【干杯】喝干杯中的酒（用于劝别人喝酒或表示庆祝的场合）"; CC-CEDICT: "Bottoms up!; lit. dry cup". How to drink only part of the glass politely (the 随意 convention, 以茶代酒 "tea instead of alcohol") was not verified in this session.

rules.rule: Hosts may urge you, repeatedly, to drink (劝酒) and to eat more. Decline with a short reason (我不会喝酒 / 开车不喝酒; 不了，我真的饱了) rather than a bare no.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 劝酒 as "（酒席上）劝人喝酒" with the example "主人举杯频频劝酒" (the host raised his glass and kept urging people to drink), and 海量 ❷ has the urging line "您是～，不妨多喝几杯" (you can hold your drink, have a few more). Food urging appears in the YCT dialogue "别客气，再吃几个饺子吧 — 不了，我真的饱了". Giving a reason is advice drawn from the sample replies, not a stated rule.

rules.rule: Let the host seat you: seats at a meal can be ranked, and it is the host who invites the guests to their seats.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 上座 = "座位分尊卑时，最尊的坐位" (when seats are ranked, the most honoured one), 首席 = the highest seat, 让座❷ = the host inviting guests to sit ("主人～又让茶"). The BCT sample above keys "可随意就座" (you may sit anywhere) as NOT the right answer. Which seat is the seat of honour (e.g. facing the door) and whether elders sit and start first were not verified in this session.

rules.rule: Leaving has a fixed exchange: the host sees you out and says 您慢走 / 您走好; you ask them not to come further (别送了 / 您留步), and they may still walk you to the bus stop.
rules.why: Official function list, section 告别: "[主人]：不远送了 [主人]：您慢走/您走好 [客人]：别送了/您留步"; XDHYCD 留步 is a 客套话 used when the host sees the guest off; HSK 5 dialogue in which the host insists on walking the guest to the bus stop.

scenes.title: Small talk with elders and answering compliments
scenes.description: Greetings (including 吃了吗), asking after an elder's health, the questions you will be asked (job, age, salary, wedding plans) with soft deflections, praising the weather and the place, and modest replies to compliments on your Chinese.

phrases.english: Have you eaten? (a greeting)
phrases.usage: A greeting, not an invitation: the official list files it under 打招呼 (greeting), marked "[吃饭前后]" (around mealtimes) and "以下多用于中国人之间" (mostly used between Chinese people). The same list notes the habit of greeting by asking about what the other person is evidently doing (上课去呀？ / 去哪儿了？ / 回来啦！). Answer briefly (我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。). How common it still is in 2026 was not checked in this session.

rules.rule: 吃了吗？ ("Have you eaten?") around mealtimes is a greeting, not an invitation; greeting someone by asking about what they are evidently doing (上课去呀？ "off to class?", 去哪儿了？ "where have you been?", 回来啦！ "you're back!") works the same way. Answer briefly (我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。).
rules.why: The official 2002 function list files these under 1. 打招呼 (greeting) with the notes "[吃饭前后]" (before/after meals), "[估计对方作什么就问什么]" (ask about what you guess the other person is doing) and "以下多用于中国人之间" (mostly used between Chinese people). How common 吃了吗 still is in 2026 was not checked.

rules.rule: Use 您 (nín, respectful "you") with your partner's parents, grandparents and other elders; they will usually call you 你.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 您 = "你；你们（含敬意）" (you, with respect), example "老师，～早！"; the polite question "您做什么工作？" is used to an adult in an HSK 2 sample. That elders use 你 to younger people is shown by the sample dialogues (e.g. "你的中文说得不错"), not stated as a rule.

rules.rule: The conventional answer to a compliment is a modest deflection: 您过奖了, 还差得远呢, 哪里哪里, or (on the formal side) 不敢当.
rules.why: The official 2002 list has a whole function "93. 谦虚" (modesty) with 哪里哪里 / 还差得远呢 / 马马虎虎吧 / 过奖了 / 不敢当; XDHYCD labels 过奖 and 哪里❺ as 谦辞 (humble words) for declining praise; the 2021 grammar standard still teaches 不敢当 (point 309, level 5: "不敢当，我只是做了我应该做的事情。"). Whether a plain 谢谢 is now just as acceptable, and whether 哪里哪里 sounds dated, was not verified in this session.

rules.rule: 你多大了 is the everyday way to ask someone's age (you will hear it). To ask an elderly person's age, the dictionary gives the honorific 高寿 (example 老大爷高寿啦？ "how old are you, grandpa?"); 贵庚 is an honorific for asking anyone's age.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 高寿 ❷ "敬辞，用于问老人的年纪"; 贵庚 "敬辞，问人年龄". 你多大了 is the everyday form (Tatoeba, HSK 1 sample). Whether younger people may ask elders with 你多大了 at all is not stated in these sources.
